validated_results.title: Food groups and renal cell carcinoma: a case-control study from Italy.
validated_results.reason: Italian hospital-based case-control study reporting a multivariate odds ratio for processed meat intake and incident, histologically confirmed renal cell carcinoma.

extraction.timing: diet assessed 2 years before diagnosis or hospital admission
extraction.population: Patients with incident histologically confirmed renal cell carcinoma and hospital controls with acute non-neoplastic conditions

sample_size.excerpt: We evaluated the relation between a wide range of foods and the risk of RCC in an Italian case-control study including 767 patients (494 men and 273 women) younger than 79 years with incident, histologically confirmed RCC, and 1,534 controls (988 men and 546 women) admitted to the same hospitals as cases for a wide spectrum of acute, non-neoplastic conditions, not related to long term diet modifications.
sample_size.location: abstract; total_n derived from reported group counts 767 + 1534 = 2301

effect_size.excerpt: Poultry (OR = 0.74), processed meat (OR = 0.64) and vegetables (OR = 0.65) were inversely associated with RCC risk.

validated_results.title: Onion and garlic use and human cancer.
validated_results.journal: The American journal of clinical nutrition
validated_results.reason: Integrated Italian and Swiss case-control studies report a multivariate odds ratio for the highest category of garlic intake and renal cell cancer.

extraction.comparison_type: highest category of garlic intake versus lowest

effect_size.excerpt: The multivariate ORs for the highest category of onion and garlic intake were, respectively, 0.16 and 0.61 for cancer of the oral cavity and pharynx, 0.12 and 0.43 for esophageal cancer, 0.44 and 0.74 for colorectal cancer, 0.17 and 0.56 for laryngeal cancer, 0.75 and 0.90 for breast cancer, 0.27 and 0.78 for ovarian cancer, 0.29 and 0.81 for prostate cancer, and 0.62 and 0.69 for renal cell cancer. This uniquely large data set from southern European populations shows an inverse association between the frequency of use of allium vegetables and the risk of several common cancers.

validated_results.title: Meat intake and bladder cancer risk in 2 prospective cohort studies.
validated_results.journal: The American journal of clinical nutrition
validated_results.reason: Two prospective cohorts examined processed meat items and incident bladder cancer, reporting a multivariate relative risk for bacon intake.

extraction.comparison_type: high bacon intake (>=5 servings/wk) versus never ate bacon
extraction.timing: pre-diagnosis, repeated food-frequency questionnaires with up to 22 y follow-up
extraction.population: Men and women in two large prospective cohorts

cases.excerpt: We analyzed data from 2 cohorts with up to 22 y of follow-up and 808 incident bladder cancer cases.

effect_size.excerpt: Men and women with a high intake of bacon (>/=5 servings/wk) had an elevated risk of bladder cancer compared with those who never ate bacon (multivariate RR = 1.59; 95% CI = 1.06, 2.37), although the overall association was not statistically significant (P for trend = 0.06). However, the association with bacon was stronger and became statistically significant after the removal of individuals who indicated having "greatly" changed their red meat (men) or bacon (women) intake during the 10 y before baseline (multivariate RR = 2.10; 95% CI = 1.24, 3.55; P for trend = 0.006).

confidence_interval.excerpt: Men and women with a high intake of bacon (>/=5 servings/wk) had an elevated risk of bladder cancer compared with those who never ate bacon (multivariate RR = 1.59; 95% CI = 1.06, 2.37), although the overall association was not statistically significant (P for trend = 0.06).
